research_question: Do the parameter-efficiency advantages observed for selected bottleneck-plus-expansion architectures persist when trained on the full MNIST training set and evaluated on the full test set?
observations: Experiment 007 placed h32_512, h64_512 and h128_512 on the accuracy-versus-parameter Pareto front.
h32_512 used 47146 parameters versus 101770 for h128 while their mean Q.ANT accuracies were 0.90400 and 0.90333 respectively in Experiment 007.
h64_512 used 88650 parameters versus 203530 for h256 while their mean Q.ANT accuracies were 0.90867 and 0.90700 respectively.
h128_512 used 171658 parameters versus 407050 for h512 while their mean Q.ANT accuracies were 0.91400 and 0.91367 respectively.
Experiment 007 used only 10000 training samples, 1000 test samples and three epochs.
hypothesis: Selected bottleneck-plus-expansion architectures will retain a parameter-efficiency advantage over matched wider single-layer controls when the experiment is scaled from the 10000/1000 MNIST subset to the full 60000/10000 MNIST dataset.
falsification: Weaken or reject the generalization claim if the selected expansion architectures lose their accuracy-versus-parameter advantage under full-dataset training, or if the matched single-layer controls become Pareto-efficient relative to them.

proposed_method.analysis: Compare mean accuracy and variability across seeds and recompute the accuracy-versus-parameter Pareto frontier under the stronger full-dataset validation regime.

limitations: The experiment still uses MNIST and therefore tests robustness within one benchmark rather than cross-dataset generalization.
Three seeds provide limited uncertainty estimation.
Q.ANT CPU backend validates execution/correctness only and does not establish photonic latency, energy efficiency, optical-noise behavior or hardware performance.
